old: Acid-catalysed hydration gives a $2^\circ$ or $3^\circ$ alcohol (Markovnikov)
new: Acid-catalysed hydration gives the Markovnikov alcohol (OH on the more substituted carbon); unsymmetrical alkenes usually give $2^\circ$ or $3^\circ$ alcohols, but ethene gives ethanol ($1^\circ$)
fixes: Hydration overgeneralised to 2°/3° alcohols; ethene gives 1° ethanol

old: In terminal alkynes, the hydrogen on the sp carbon (50% s character) is acidic, because the conjugate base carbanion is held close to the nucleus. Ethyne therefore reacts with $Na$ or $NaNH_2$ to form sodium acetylide and liberate $H_2$, which alkenes and alkanes cannot do. Terminal alkynes also give a white precipitate with ammoniacal $AgNO_3$ and a red precipitate with ammoniacal $Cu_2Cl_2$. Internal alkynes have no acidic hydrogen. Alkynes undergo addition reactions in which two molecules of reagent can add. They take up $H_2$ (Lindlar's catalyst gives a cis alkene, $Na$/liquid $NH_3$ gives a trans alkene, and $Pt$/$Ni$ goes all the way to the alkane). They decolourise $Br_2$ and add $HX$ by Markovnikov's rule to give gem-dihalides. Hydration with $HgSO_4$/dil. $H_2SO_4$ at 333 K proceeds via an enol to give a carbonyl compound. Linear polymerisation of ethyne gives polyacetylene, a conducting polymer. Cyclic polymerisation (red-hot iron tube, 873 K) gives benzene.
new: In terminal alkynes, the hydrogen on the sp carbon (50% s character) is acidic, because the conjugate base carbanion is held close to the nucleus. Ethyne therefore reacts with $Na$ to form sodium acetylide and liberate $H_2$, and with $NaNH_2$ to form sodium acetylide and $NH_3$, which alkenes and alkanes cannot do. Alkynes undergo addition reactions in which two molecules of reagent can add. They decolourise $Br_2$ and add $HX$ by Markovnikov's rule to give gem-dihalides. Hydration with $HgSO_4$/dil. $H_2SO_4$ at 333 K proceeds via an enol to give a carbonyl compound. fixes: H2 liberated only with Na; NaNH2 gives NH3
